claim: For every natural n whose sum 1 + ... + n fits in i64, sum-to's body takes n to that sum within 14n + 10 steps at kernel cost at most 13n + 10, with no i64 overflow on the way.

For every integer x whose negation is in i64 (-(2^63 - 1) <= x <= 2^63, so every i64 value except -2^63), abs's body takes x to its absolute value within 16 steps at kernel cost at most 15, with no i64 overflow on the way.
For all integers a and b with b nonzero and the quotient a div b in i64, divmod's body takes a b to the Euclidean quotient and remainder (0 <= a mod b < |b|) in exactly 6 steps at kernel cost 6.

For all a and b in i64 whose greatest common divisor is in i64 (every pair except those with gcd 2^63: -2^63 0, 0 -2^63 and -2^63 -2^63), gcd's body takes a b to their greatest common divisor within 22|b| + 33 steps at kernel cost at most 20|b| + 31 (a linear bound, looser than Euclid's logarithmic one), with no i64 overflow on the way.

For every stock available, policy whole (true for all-or-nothing), flat ID sequence ids and quantities qs with ids.length = 4 * qs.length and every entry of ids in [0, 65^8) (IdParts: the host's encoding of each ID as four eight-digit base-65 parts), and with no bound assumed on available or the quantities, allocate-batch's body leaves batchSpec: code 1 with 0, [], [] when the input is outside the spec's bounds (0 <= available <= 1,000,000, at most 64 requests, each quantity from 1 to 1,000,000); otherwise code 2 with 0, [], [] when two requests' four-part ID blocks are equal; otherwise code 0 with Spec.allocateAll's remaining stock, allocations and reason codes. It does so within 181 + 224n + 172·n(n−1)/2 steps at kernel cost at most 165 + 202n + 163·n(n−1)/2 for n = qs.length, with no i64 overflow on the way.
